name: Kaluza-Klein Black Holes
description: The charged black holes of gravity in five dimensions with the fifth dimension a small circle, vacuum solutions that four dimensions see as black holes with an electric charge, a magnetic charge, or both, and a scalar field. The electric hole is Schwarzschild's black string set moving around the circle, and Gary Gibbons and David Wiltshire classified the family in 1986.
convention: The lengths $r_s$, $q$, and $p$ fix the mass and the charges. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: How do you charge a black hole when you have no electric field to charge it with? Theodor Kaluza found Maxwell's equations inside general relativity written in five dimensions, and Oskar Klein rolled the fifth dimension into a circle too small to see [kaluza1921, klein1926, duff1994]. A black hole in that world can be Schwarzschild's at every point of the circle, a black string [horowitz2012]. Set the string moving around the circle and it becomes a charged black hole for anyone too large to see the circle, since "the four dimensional charge is simply the five dimensional momentum" [horowitz2012]. Nothing was added to make the charge: in five dimensions the moving string still solves the vacuum equations [horowitz2012].¶The horizon and the singularity of the moving string stay where Schwarzschild's are, at $r = r_s$ and $r = 0$ [horowitz2012]. For a boost of rapidity $\alpha$ the line element is $$ds^2 = -\left(1 - \frac{q}{r}\right)c^2dt^2 - \frac{2\sqrt{q(q - r_s)}}{r}\,c\,dt\,dy + \left(1 + \frac{q - r_s}{r}\right)dy^2 + \left(1 - \frac{r_s}{r}\right)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2,$$ with $q = r_s\cosh^2\alpha$ and $y$ the coordinate around the circle [horowitz2012]. Four dimensions read it as a metric, a Maxwell potential, and a scalar field that records the length of the circle, which grows toward the hole [horowitz2012]. Reissner and Nordström's charged hole has an inner horizon, and this one has none [horowitz2012]. Its charge can approach twice that of an extremal Reissner-Nordström hole of the same mass, and at that limit the horizon has shrunk onto the singularity and the string moves at the speed of light, a gravitational wave in five dimensions [horowitz2012, rasheed1995].¶All the stationary, spherically symmetric solutions of Kaluza and Klein's theory were written down in 1982 by P. Dobiasch and Dieter Maison, with the conditions under which they are black holes with mass, electric charge, and magnetic charge [dobiasch1982]. The same year brought the most general time independent, spherically symmetric solution of the vacuum equations in five dimensions, from Alan Chodos and Steven Detweiler [chodos1982]. A year later David Pollard exhibited dyonic black holes with scalar charge, which "share some similarities with the extreme Reissner-Nordstrom black holes of Einstein-Maxwell theory" [pollard1983]. Gary Gibbons and David Wiltshire put the family in order in 1986: they classified the solutions that are regular black holes in four dimensions and worked out their thermodynamics [gibbonswiltshire1986].¶Trade the electric charge for a magnetic one and the metric of four dimensions stays as it was, while the fifth dimension changes [horowitz2012]. The circle is now twisted over each sphere by the potential of a magnetic monopole, and it shrinks toward the hole [horowitz2012]. Take the horizon away, $r_s = 0$, and the hole is the Kaluza-Klein monopole of David Gross, Malcolm Perry, and Rafael Sorkin, smooth at the point where the circle closes [horowitz2012, grossperry1983, sorkin1983]. Four dimensions see a singularity at that point, which makes the monopole "a four dimensional spacetime with curvature singularity that is resolved by lifting the solution to five dimensions" [horowitz2012]. Where does a magnetic hole go as it evaporates? Gibbons and Wiltshire expected "an evolution towards the extreme configuration corresponding to the Gross-Perry-Sorkin monopole" [gibbonswiltshire1986].¶And a hole with both charges? With the two equal it is consistent to hold the scalar field constant, so the circle keeps one length everywhere and the metric of four dimensions is Reissner and Nordström's [larsen2000]. A hole with both charges has an extremal limit with a smooth horizon of nonzero area [horowitz2012]. The extremal holes lie on the astroid $(Q/M)^{2/3} + (P/M)^{2/3} = 2^{2/3}$ in units with $G = c = 1$, and those of Reissner and Nordström on a circle [rasheed1995]. The whole family with rotation is Dean Rasheed's, and the lengths $p$ and $q$ used here are Finn Larsen's [rasheed1995, larsen2000].¶In string theory the two charges have names: with six more small dimensions and the circle taken as the circle of M theory, the electric charge is that of D0-branes and the magnetic charge that of D6-branes, so Larsen read the holes as bound states of the two [larsen2000]. In D-branes Roberto Emparan and Horowitz found a description that reproduces the entropy of a hole with both charges at its extremal limit, "even though supersymmetry is completely broken" [emparan2006]. A black string carrying momentum around the circle is unstable as the string at rest is: Jordan Hovdebo and Robert Myers found the Gregory-Laflamme instability in it, with "a simple kinematical relation between the thresholds" of the boosted string and the static one [hovdebo2006].

related.text: The hole with no charge, $q = r_s$ and $p = r_s$: Schwarzschild's black hole at every point of the circle. Set it moving around the circle and it is the electric hole [horowitz2012].
The magnetic hole with its horizon taken away, $r_s = 0$, where $p = 4m$. The circle then closes smoothly at $r = 0$ and no singularity is left [horowitz2012].
With equal electric and magnetic charges the scalar field is constant, and the metric orthogonal to the circles is Reissner and Nordström's, with both of its horizons [larsen2000].

The charged black hole of string theory, whose scalar field couples to the Maxwell field with strength $1$ where Kaluza and Klein's couples with strength $\sqrt{3}$. Gibbons and Maeda found the charged holes for every coupling [gibbons1988, rasheed1995].

The electric hole at the speed of light, $r_s = 0$ with $q$ held fixed, is a plane fronted wave in five dimensions with the profile $q/r$, the counterpart there of Aichelburg and Sexl's shock [horowitz2012].

coordinates.name: Electric Charge

parameters.description: Radius of the horizon, the Schwarzschild radius of the black string before the boost

Charge length, $q = r_s\cosh^2\alpha$ for a boost of rapidity $\alpha$ along the circle; $q \ge r_s$, and $q = r_s$ is no charge. In units with $G = c = 1$ in four dimensions the mass is $M = (q + r_s)/4$ and the electric charge $Q = \sqrt{q(q - r_s)}/2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi, y)$, Schwarzschild's with the length $y$ around the fifth dimension added, and $t$ carrying dimensions of time. The circle of $y$ has any length $L$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{t} + \dfrac{q}{r\left(r - r_s\right)}\dot{t}\dot{r} - \dfrac{\sqrt{q}\sqrt{q - r_s}}{r\left(r - r_s\right)}\dot{r}\dot{y} = 0

\ddot{r} + \dfrac{q\left(r - r_s\right)}{2r^3}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{\sqrt{q}\sqrt{q - r_s}\left(r - r_s\right)}{r^3}\dot{t}\dot{y} - \dfrac{r_s}{2r\left(r - r_s\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \left(r - r_s\right)\dot{\theta}^2 - \left(r - r_s\right)\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 + \dfrac{\left(q - r_s\right)\left(r - r_s\right)}{2r^3}\dot{y}^2 = 0
\ddot{\theta} + \dfrac{2}{r}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} - \sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
\ddot{\phi} + \dfrac{2}{r}\dot{r}\dot{\phi} + 2\cot\theta\,\dot{\theta}\dot{\phi} = 0
\ddot{y} + \dfrac{\sqrt{q}\sqrt{q - r_s}}{r\left(r - r_s\right)}\dot{t}\dot{r} - \dfrac{q - r_s}{r\left(r - r_s\right)}\dot{r}\dot{y} = 0

\ddot{r} + \dfrac{q\left(r - r_s\right)}{2r^3}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{\sqrt{q}\sqrt{r_s}}{r^2}\dot{v}\dot{r} - \dfrac{\sqrt{q}\sqrt{q - r_s}\left(r - r_s\right)}{r^3}\dot{v}\dot{w} + \dfrac{\sqrt{r_s}\sqrt{q - r_s}}{r^2}\dot{r}\dot{w} - \left(r - r_s\right)\dot{\theta}^2 - \left(r - r_s\right)\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 + \dfrac{\left(q - r_s\right)\left(r - r_s\right)}{2r^3}\dot{w}^2 = 0
\ddot{\theta} + \dfrac{2}{r}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} - \sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
\ddot{\phi} + \dfrac{2}{r}\dot{r}\dot{\phi} + 2\cot\theta\,\dot{\theta}\dot{\phi} = 0

\ddot{w} + \dfrac{q\,\sqrt{q - r_s}}{2r^2\,\sqrt{r_s}}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{\sqrt{q}\left(q - r_s\right)}{r^2\,\sqrt{r_s}}\dot{v}\dot{w} - \dfrac{r\,\sqrt{q - r_s}}{\sqrt{r_s}}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r\,\sqrt{q - r_s}\sin^2\theta}{\sqrt{r_s}}\dot{\phi}^2 + \dfrac{\left(q - r_s\right)^{3/2}}{2r^2\,\sqrt{r_s}}\dot{w}^2 = 0
